speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are also now seeing the complex dynamics of multiple dimensions, such as climate change and public health, being interconnected with food resilience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is already evident in some of the objectives of the Bill, which includes safeguarding against potential supply disruptions and enabling MOH to promote public health through better diet and nutrition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is time that we do more than merely to support local.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It means listening to the needs of all players across the agri-food value chain, to introduce policies that actively address these needs, while being a part of a holistic strategy built upon strengthening food resilience, and not just leave it to the vagaries of consumer sentiment to bring about genuine change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also means recognising and harnessing strengths of our local produce, championing them and not merely seeing local produce as a charity course to be supported.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this vein, two main groups I would like to speak on are: first, food producers or farmers; and second, consumers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For food producers, current strategies revolve around helping farms grow more with less.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Policy examples include the unlocking of land and sea space, and co-funding schemes such as the Agriculture Productivity Fund for high tech productive farming systems.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is much emphasis on farming technology and research and development.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, this means that we might sometimes lose sight of the unviable economics that most farms in Singapore currently face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need policies based on first principles in order to mitigate the large cost buckets for operating a farm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can we streamline administrative hurdles in order for farmers to, for example, tap into renewable energy options such as solar panel installations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the Bill contains provisions relating to an MSR to secure our own supply of food sources, which is important, given the rise in protectionist sentiments globally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clauses 28 to 31 further describe the obligations that MSR entities are under and the penalties that they are subject to should they fail to adhere to the directives given to them by the DG (FS).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is thus concern amongst food producers and other players about which foods will fall under the MSR framework, and that this will add to additional compliance and other costs, particularly for SMEs or startups in the space.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could there be more specific guidance given to industry players over the short to medium term about what foods will likely be considered as MSR products?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, what assistance, be they financial subsidies, shared infrastructure will be made available to support any additional costs associated with being subject to the MSR regime?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, we understand that the previous rice stockpile scheme will come under this MSR.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But beyond rice, should we consider an MSR for seed storage, given how prone seeds are to supply chain disruptions, and as a lifeblood for each harvest.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we are serious about achieving our 30 by 30 goal and more, should we also not critically evaluate the 1% of land allocated for agricultural land use in Singapore against other competing land use needs?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: SFA aims to raise awareness on food security issues and rally support for local produce by encouraging consumers to make environmentally sustainable food choices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially given how food systems account for one third of global greenhouse gas emissions and food miles account for 19% of those emissions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Minister herself echoed this narrative by calling on Singaporeans in April 2023 to support local, even if it costs more than imported produce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, a survey conducted by UGov in 2024 found that only between a third to just under half of consumers expressed a preference to buy local eggs, vegetables or seafood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Of those who did not currently prefer to buy local produce, over eight in 10 Singaporeans said that they would likely switch to buying local if prices were lower than imported produce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While there are undoubtedly factors that may prompt Singaporeans to support locals, such as safety and freshness, it appears that cost remains a barrier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Rallying and nudging Singaporeans to support local will not be sufficient in itself if we were to spur demand on a long-term sustainable basis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How then can we build the right demand conditions to allow our agri-food sector to thrive?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Greater subsidies for local farms, and/or the imposition of import taxes could help, but if we want to achieve our food security goal, we have to sustainably tackle the issue of cost.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In light of this, I have some questions on the topic of cost premiums associated with local produce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The tiered Farm to Table Recognition Programme (FTTRP) recognises businesses that produce at least 15% of local produce in at least one food category from a list of six categories, or the roughly 70 establishments that are on the FTTRP benefit from exposure and publicity in the hotels, restaurants and catering sector, there is little by way of encouraging eventual demand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can the qualifying criteria for the programme be strengthened over time in order to increase producer offtake?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Simultaneously, can there be preferential credits or tax relief that can translate into local costs for end consumers dining at FTTRP recognised establishments?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just like in any industry, local farms operate in an individualistic competitive environment, facing both local and foreign competition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While there are benefits in having a free and open market, the issue of strengthening food resilience begs the question of whether such an approach will continue to be in our best interest in the long term.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can we explore cooperative structures for local farmers in order to mitigate key challenges, especially in the key cost buckets of energy, manpower and rent?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To be sure, Singapore is not the only urban centre facing the challenge of encouraging eating local, especially where there are budgetary constraints.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More specifically, while there have been tentative steps in starting community supported agriculture in Singapore, it would be remiss of us not to learn from where this has worked and the potential pitfalls experienced by other countries in this model of farming.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, food and nutrition are intrinsically linked to public health, and every human being should have a right to access healthy and fresh food or produce that is not cost prohibitive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so given the increasing awareness and research about the severe health risks associated with the consumption of ultra processed foods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This calls for new intervention models and multi-sector collaboration for food support between the Government, non-profit and private sector, and we have every reason for local produce to form the pillar of such models.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, what does it mean to champion local?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It means we must be prepared to challenge prevailing strategies, approaches and tools at our disposal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It means for us to look to a cooperative mindset as a collective whole.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It means that we start from a young age and ensure that our young ones understand both the challenges and benefits of eating local, particularly in a world facing a climate emergency.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Most of all, it involves addressing the targeted needs of each stakeholder, in order to build a food system that champions local, boosts demand for local, while ensuring that vulnerable low-income households can also benefit from having affordable access to fresh and healthy local produce.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: According to the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations, food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Approximately one-third of all food produced globally is wasted.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As a small nation highly dependent on food imports, ensuring less wastage while diversifying food sources locally, will help to bolster our food security.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With the diversity of food sources, it is, therefore, necessary to ensure that food is safe for consumption, no matter how it reaches us; whether we purchase it as consumers, receive it through the goodwill of donations, or participate in community initiatives like neighbourhood food distributions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Community gardens and localised food production initiatives, not only supplement fresh produce supply but also foster a sense of community ownership and responsibility over food resources.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Useful resources, such as "A resource guide for community gardeners" by the American Community Gardening Association, suggest that increasing access to fresh produce can strengthen the role of enhancing food security at the local level.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Research also supported the findings that individuals who engage in gardening activities experience an increased physical activity, and contributes to better overall health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In light of case studies from urban farming projects like ComCrop and Edible Gardens Singapore, can SFA share what is its position on community-based local farming on a small-scale for local sharing?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As my colleagues are aware, many of our neighbourhoods have community gardens, which often yield a variety of produce that is generously shared among residents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I would like to understand SFA's position on community-based local farming on a small-scale for local sharing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can SFA elaborate on what are some guidelines or regulations it plans to implement, if any, for community grown and shared food?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am keen to understand the science and rationale behind this policy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, chickens have been traditionally used in many farms in kampongs; they are excellent natural workers that help till the soil and provide organic fertiliser.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this because I am aware that NParks expends regularly significant resources to manage wild chicken populations in various neighbourhoods due to residents' feedback about loud roosters crowing at early hours.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than focusing on culling, could there be a more innovative and sustainable solution to redirect these chickens for local farming efforts?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Might it not be a good idea to deploy them to community gardens instead – perhaps, minus the roosters?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, some people I know have innovatively fashioned soundproof coops with repurposed construction sound barrier material – the ones that you see outside of construction projects – to prevent noise disamenity from the roosters.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This is a good way of repurposing materials.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: According to permaculture practitioners worldwide, sharing their experiences online, one backyard chicken can effectively till 50 square feet of soil in just a few weeks while providing nitrogen that enhances soil health for better yields.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This farming method, rooted in sustainable, low-input techniques, is both environmentally friendly and resource-efficient; and the children love them!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am personally involved in advocating and implementing permaculture farming within my constituency in Nee Soon South.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We collaborate with like-minded citizens who are helping Singaporeans learn about food growing cycles with a focus on reducing food waste, promoting sustainable practices and fostering community engagement in urban farming.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these efforts have successfully actualised circular economy principles, such as recollect used coffee grounds from nearby coffee shops and viable kitchen scraps from residents for composting.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Community gardens can be co-designed and re-imagined to play a vital role in promoting sustainable practices, such as composting and water conservation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These gardens serve as educational spaces, teaching residents about the importance of environmental stewardship.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Actually, anyone who is interested and everyone who would like to come and visit our Khatib Wellspring Farmden at Blk 783, Yishun Ring Road, can come any Sunday between 9.00 am and 3.00 pm to see these principles in action.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: A vibrant ecosystem with diverse plant and animal species working symbiotically offers wonderful opportunities for children and adults to learn about the interdependence of various living beings within the web of life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It makes our neighbourhoods come alive and helps alleviate climate anxiety because people feel more secure knowing that Mother Nature blesses us with abundance when we learn to care for and work with her.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am not saying this as a theory.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This is actual feedback shared by young people from Singapore University of Social Sciences who collaborated with us and participated in our Famden in permaculture, in order to help us with a public education campaign.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They shared that being hands on with growing food and seeing the community actively doing so, helped to alleviate their anxiety about climate change and climate crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to share an interesting piece of history I came across in my research.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Did you know that during World War II, many countries including the UK, Canada, Australia, Germany and the US promoted backyard gardening and chicken rearing to ensure food sufficiency for their war efforts?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These initiatives were known as "Victory Gardens", encouraging citizens to grow food in backyards, rooftops, window boxes and vacant public lots.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can take a leaf out of this book, because now, with the fossil fuel shortage, we can also look into how hyper local farming and hyper local food sources can help to reduce the carbon footprint of our food chain.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While we are not at war now, and I hope we never will be, it does not mean we cannot learn from this historical context.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In true Singaporean spirit of "kiasu", fear of losing, and "kiasi", fear of death, I see no harm in cultivating our citizens' green fingers en masse.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It might come in handy one day, in creating viable hyper local community food gardens that can help to mitigate any supply chain crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There is a growing community of nature and permaculture enthusiasts who genuinely wish to contribute to Singapore's food resilience.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Understanding SFA's stance on this matter, would be beneficial as we forge alliances toward our common goals related to food resilience and safety.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can grow our collective knowledge and evolve Singapore's food system into a more inclusive and resilient one, enabling community-based food growing efforts to grow at scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I welcome the introduction of this Bill, I do have some questions for the Minister and I would like to share some concerns.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome the change in law providing for the increased flexibility for Singaporeans to import food of all types, save for a few specific items like animal blood.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For personal consumption, limited to 15 kilogrammes, doing away with existing rules, allowing Singaporeans to, say, bring home meat products from certain countries alone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I think the rule change makes good sense and allows Singaporeans to make decisions for themselves for their own personal consumption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recall that on a constituency trip to Johor last year, a resident of mine happily bought a number of rice dumplings with pork, intending for family members to enjoy having first tried one and found them to be good.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But she had to share the dumplings with fellow travellers for consumption before coming back to Singapore when she found out that she was not allowed to bring the dumplings into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know the tiering and enhancing of penalties and the strengthening of food safety regulatory framework beyond increasing penalties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister share with this House, what are the other efforts of SFA to promote best practices in the industry and minimise incidents of food poisoning?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How can SFA engender a deeper appreciation of good food safety practices and ingrain a strong food safety culture among caterers and workers in the industry?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Shortly after that, at the Committee of Supply debates in March 2019, the then Minister for the Environment and Water Resources, Mr Masagos Zulkifli, told Parliament about SFA's grow local strategy to, I quote, "reduce our reliance on imports and buffer the impact of overseas supply disruptions".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last August, Senior Minister of State, Dr Koh Poh Koon, replied to Parliamentary Questions from myself and other Members of this House on the 30 by 30 vision, and gave some updates on our efforts to achieve the 30 by 30 vision.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Among other things, he mentioned that the business climate has, since 2019, become less favourable due to factors such as COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions and inflation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He mentioned that during COVID-19 pandemic, an initial phase of reopening, our farms face a shortage of foreign workers and construction delays, and in a post pandemic period, inflation and energy price highs exacerbated by geopolitical tensions, as well as a more challenging financial environment have added to their challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It cannot be, because we need now more than before, to press on towards the goal in the next five years, in spite of the challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the geopolitical economy and landscape now, more than before, we need to use to use Minister Masagos' words from five years ago to, I quote, "strengthen climate resilience and overcome our resource constraints." Mr Speaker, many felt that the recently concluded 29th Conference of the Parties (COP29) have focused more on securing agreement for the carbon credit issue over the need to reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At its current pace, the world's current Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) lead to about 2.7°C warming, far from the 1.5°C Paris Agreement target.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Falling short of this target for 2030 is worrying for the world and for Singapore, as climate changes are ever visible everywhere in the world with more frequent and unexpected bad weather or serious weather pattern changes, including floods, droughts and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One important consequence we are starting to see is how climate changes more frequently and adversely affect farming output, including aquaculture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The recent crop failures of cocoa and coffee beans worldwide leading to massive increase in prices is a good reminder of how climate changes can affect worldwide supply and pricing of staple foods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Temperature rises and lack of rainfall in Brazil led to price increase of Arabica coffee beans from US$1.5 per pound in October 2023 to US$2.5 per pound in July 2024.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Price of Robusta coffee beans rose from US$2.60 per kilogramme in July 2023 to US$4.68 per kilogramme a year later due to one of the worst droughts in Vietnam.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even rice, which is a stockpile item under the MSR in this current Bill, is highly vulnerable to climate change as it requires a high amount of water, is unable to withstand any drought and can only grow between 21°C to 37°C.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Temperatures, in fact, above 35°C, can adversely affect yields.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the current global warming trajectory of 2.7°C, one cannot rule out rice yields being affected by weather changes in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many smaller states are disproportionately affected by climate change, as compared to bigger countries who have greater means and may prioritise their own climate change interest ahead of others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some progress, but arguably insufficient for the Paris goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this post-COVID world, the continual rise of protectionism worldwide, coupled with the lack of enforceable global frameworks, may likely see countries prioritising self-preservation and self-interest, leaving vulnerable small states like Singapore, who requires import of most of our food needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If food-producing countries are affected by crop failures or declines brought about by climate changes, there may not be sufficient food exports and countries like Singapore will suffer by the drop in supply or even significant price increases, which will also bring financial hardship to our people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Likewise, geopolitical conflicts or tensions may also affect food production and exports, leading to similar consequences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In short, the above circumstances underlie the increased importance of food security for Singapore in an increasingly uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I can agree that the MSR regime will, in principle, be able to provide us with short-term food supply, especially in times of crisis, when for political or environmental reasons, fresh supplies of food are suddenly cut off from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would the MSR regime eventually cover a full range of food items, providing for adequate nutritional and calorific requirements for every adult and child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I heard Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon said in his speech just now that it will only be rice now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But what are the conditions that will enable the DG to decide on other food categories to be included under this regime?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill also does not explicitly specify the required levels or thresholds under the MSR regime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such risks can include pandemics, geopolitical tensions, export bans and climate-related shocks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister share with the House what are the expected levels of stockpiling required under the MSR regime?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Government to give some details to give assurance to Singaporeans of the sufficiency of the MSR stockpiles in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, the MSR regime may impose significant burden on our food suppliers and importers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Bill is imposing penalties on businesses under the MSR regime, has the Government studied the financial impact the MSR regime may have on our Singapore suppliers and importers, especially our SMEs and local businesses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will financial assistance, by way of grants or subsidies be given to SMEs to help them to comply with the MSR stockpile requirements?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond financial assistance for the additional stocks required to be stockpiled by businesses under the MSR regime, will the Government also provide direct financial assistance by way of grants or subsidies, or even actual warehouse space for the additional storage space for the mandated stockpile so that businesses will not be out of pocket.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is pertinent that Government should take steps to ensure that all compliant costs will not be passed on to the ultimate consumes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh replied that SFA ensures that the ACT Fund remains relevant in meeting farms, business and growth needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh also said that the ACT Fund encourages our farms to invest in productive and resource-efficient technologies that can help to manage resource use and consequently, operating costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He added that the SFA introduced the Energy Efficiency Programme in 2023 under this Fund to co-fund energy efficiency audits and adoption of energy-efficient equipment and technologies to help our farms better manage their energy costs for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I am sure that the ACT Fund has helped some businesses, I urge the Government to also consider giving assistance beyond capital expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may be for farms which are not necessarily high technology or require assistance outside of technology or capability upgrades.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Labour and rental costs are always a bugbear in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh, in a reply to another Member of this House in August, was vehement against directly offsetting operating expenses, stating, and I quote, "It will be something quite challenging because it could well end up having the perverse effect of paying for inefficient players offset their costs to the detriment of taxpayers money as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, we want to fund them so that whatever they do has durability and sustainability for the longer term and fundamentally changes the way the company operates for more sustainable future." I understand this reasoning, but I still hope that the Government can do more to help our agri-businesses who are impacted by high operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unlike other business sectors, the Government needs to find different ways to help our farms and agri-trade businesses to produce sufficiently so that they can, in turn, help Singapore to achieve the 30 by 30 vision for our food security.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How can the Government do more to help our farms and businesses to supply the required products, given weather and other environmental constraints, higher production, labour and rental costs, which may make their products more expensive as compared to the same products from another country?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It would not be just any type of vegetables or fish that is easy and cheaper to grow or breed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our farm must supply part of the common basic food choices required by our own consumers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This can be seen in the EU member countries – Japan, Canada and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Granted that our agriculture is on a different scale compared to these countries, but a little more help to our farms and businesses, where possible, even not on the same scale, can still help to push the needle for food security.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One of our residents has asked about the effectiveness of the current measure as taken by the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He asked that if the current Government initiatives are adequate or productive, why are local farms still struggling and, in some cases closing down?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, those who are struggling or closing down, they cannot all be inefficient players.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our resident has also asked what are the additional steps which can be taken to ensure the sustainability and growth of local farms and whether there are gaps in the current approach that needs to be addressed to better support our local producers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The same issues of food security for crops will also affect the security of seeds, feed and fertiliser.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Without security of supply with stable pricing, this will also affect the ability of our agri-businesses to secure their production and ultimately, supply of food to Singaporeans, not to mention the survival of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, there should be more bottom-up conversations with all stakeholders in the food sector to identify the pain points that each is facing, whether in farming, supplying or in procuring local produce.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The additional points increase their chances of securing Government catering contracts, including those with key Government entities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome these and other efforts she shared.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These institutional buyers supply food to key government entities like the Singapore Armed Forces, public hospitals, Prisons, welfare homes and senior care centres and play critical roles in scaling demand for domestic food.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Minister Grace Fu also said our local agri-food sector also depends on consumer demand for their products, that consumers can play a part by choosing to purchase local produce, which can be easily recognised by the red SG Fresh Produce logo or on dine and food businesses under the FTTRP.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I strongly agree with her when she said that local produce, I quote, "Local produce is fresher, lasts longer and incurs less transport miles as it need not travel long miles or for long periods of time before reaching customers." For many years, this adage of incurring less air miles has been in our minds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Whenever my wife and I are buying groceries, we may not always be able to avoid buying foods from afar, but it does help to steer decisions to buy local products whenever they are available.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Less air miles, my wife will always remind me.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This should complement the new MSR regime, setting up food stockpiles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a timely and necessary step to ensure Singapore's resilience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the public remains deeply concerned about food safety, especially following last year's high-profile mass food poisoning cases affecting preschools and corporations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Parents, in particular, worry about the safety of their children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there provisions to address systemic gaps in hygiene practices or monitoring?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, while penalties serve as a deterrent, how does the Ministry determine their calibration to ensure they are neither excessively punitive for small businesses nor too lenient to deter large offenders?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For small food businesses, the transition to the new safety regime will likely result in increased compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may disproportionately impact small operators, leading to challenges in adapting or passing costs on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the SFA provide guidance, subsidies or transitional support to ease their burden?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Food recalls, even when not caused by negligence, can severely disrupt small businesses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Training is essential to ensuring proper food handling practices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If individual accountability is removed, how will the SFA enforce compliance and incentivise food business licensees to send their workers for training?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Should not both businesses and workers be held accountable to uphold food safety standards?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What measures will the Ministry implement to prevent the entry of contaminated or non-compliant food products?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will enhanced screening or consumer education be part of this change?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, home-based food businesses represent an important source of livelihood for many.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, these enterprises are not, currently, required to obtain licenses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the SFA work with these businesses to encourage food safety training and refresher courses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could we provide affordable training options or incentives to raise safety standards across all food operators?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Addressing these concerns will ensure that the new framework enhances food safety without undue burdens on Singaporeans as well as the small business owners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As important, the Bill reconciles new needs that emerge because of dynamic travel and trade landscapes and the evergreen priorities of food safety and food resilience.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, I seek clarity on three areas of impact to consumers and workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare that I am also the Executive Secretary of the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union, the union for persons working in accommodation and food sectors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, section 124 outlines the direction for food vending machines and other equipment in respect of food safety.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on the type of checks that the authorised officer or food inspector might undertake to determine if a food vending machine is in unclean or unsanitary condition as to make any food obtained from the machine unsafe or unsuitable, or likely to be unsafe or unsuitable?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To help consumers to exercise safe consumption, SFA might wish to consider requiring vending machine operators to display on a conspicuous part of the machine, the most recent date the machine was cleaned; and for highly perishable foods, such as cut-fruit, the "sell-by" date.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the explanatory notes on Part 4 of the Bill had stated, "Part 4 moves more towards emphasising preventative measures devised by the food business licensees themselves for ensuring food safety and hygiene along the licensee's entire food handling process." Under this shift, some food businesses could be required to implement a food control plan of preventative measures, such as tailored safety and hygiene conditions and specific training plans for staff, to ensure the safety and suitability of the food in a food business' production process.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Food businesses must also be able to trace food one step backwards and one step forwards.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, implementing these requirements could also be a tall order given the state of churn of food businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, could the Minister share SFA's plans to ensure that persons setting up food businesses are made aware of the new requirements and geared up to implement the requirements, such as putting in place the training and processes to ensure that their workforce can implement and upkeep the requirements?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Last, in respect of section 92 that outlines the criteria for grant of food business license.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Especially if the applicant is intending to enter the food services sector, a sector under the progressive wage model, where practices must be strengthened if the sector is to be able to uplift Singaporean workers' skills and wages and enhance worker's safety and health.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, the Bill is timely and commendable.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It charts the way forward for Singapore and its agri-food supply chain stakeholders and consumers to embrace a food safety culture and be assured of food security and resilience for the long-term.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the Food Safety and Security Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill will update and consolidate existing rules and regulations related to food safety and security.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With an overall framework, SFA can better strengthen and enforce the system for regulating food safety to protect public health.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What factors will the authorities consider when implementing the new requirements?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill aims to improve the level of procurement and production safety in the food industry, and also to increase the accountability of industry organisations in handling food, including record traceability, submission of food control plans and feed control plans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does SFA have for the challenges and problems they will face?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any measures to help the industry, especially small companies, adapt to the transition period and meet the requirements of the new food safety system?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Food safety practices have contributed to the success of food-based businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans, residents and visitors can be assured that operators are required, by law, to observe standards and practices that ensure all food sold is safe for consumption.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While the barrier to entry for establishing a food business is low, the basic licensing requirements hold operators responsible and accountable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The rationale to exclude home-based food business from requiring licensing relates to the scale of operations, being a smaller scale operation and, therefore, the resulting lower risk in the area of food safety issues.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Home-based food business is a helpful means, both as primary and supplementary sources of income.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It also presents a low-cost means to test out whether a food and beverage concept or model is viable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad the Government agencies continue to keep a light touch on this group of operators.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One result of this light touch is the lack of data, as anyone can start a home-based food business.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If so, are there any upper limits on the number of home-based food businesses an individual or family can operate without the requirement to be licensed?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear that home-based food business must adhere to proper food safety practices and will be subject to enforcement should lapses occur.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It would, therefore, be helpful for food-based operators to access courses on best practices relating to food safety and hygiene.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Whether the food business requires a licence or is exempt, it would certainly be in the interest of the operator to observe proper safety standards for the business to thrive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill seeks to streamline some of the processes and also reduce compliances costs for food businesses that do require licensing.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This is welcome news for an industry facing many areas of cost increases.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Food operators should remain responsible in ensuring that the food safety standards are not diminished.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are currently progressing toward our goal of producing 30% of our annual requirements by 2030.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Food businesses are prepared to play an increasing part in providing demand for local produce by including locally-sourced or grown products in the primary ingredients.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, consumers are also willing to switch to local produce to bring the local supply chain to financially sustainable levels.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While some food operators have introduced successful farm to table or farm to fork concepts, these tend to be at the higher price end.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For operators whose concepts fall more in the mass market, or middle or lower price end, there are possibly two factors currently limiting the switch to local produce.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One is the matter of price as local produce will compete with produce from other sources of supply.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The other is the ability to supply in sufficient quantities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Also, will food operators who support local suppliers be considered for some form of support or subsidy until suppliers can reach economies of scale and, therefore, become more price competitive?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some Members have also sought clarifications, which largely revolve around three themes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, how the Bill will consolidate and enhance food safety requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I will address clarifications on how these apply for certain types of food businesses, worker training and food recalls, while the Minister will address clarifications relating to the supply of food, such as implications for donated food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, how the Bill will help us prepare for emerging challenges in safeguarding food security.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I will address questions about the MSR and FMP.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Third, how we will support the industry and collaborate with stakeholders in the transition towards the updated food safety and security regime.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, on how the FSSB will consolidate and enhance food safety requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng said there might be subjectivity in determining novel foods as defined in the Bill and asked if the Ministry could provide more guidance on this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He also asked about plans for publicity and education to the industry and consumers on defined foods that have obtained pre-market approval.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The safety assessments should cover potential food safety risks such as toxicity, allergenicity, safety of the production methods used and dietary exposure arising from consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To assist companies in this journey, SFA has published and regularly updates the guidance document on novel food safety assessment requirements on its website.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Companies can also consult SFA or sign up for the bi-monthly Novel Food Virtual Clinics to better understand SFA's requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA will continue to ensure that sufficient clarity is provided to industry through direct engagements with novel food companies, as well as through the updating of guidance documents online.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Following pre-market approval, the novel food at hand will no longer remain as a defined food and can be made available for consumption as food by the general public.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA currently already publishes information on approved GM food and will also be publishing information on the identities of approved novel foods on its website.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is intended to help interested consumers and industry better identify these approved novel food and GM food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee asked how SFA will work with home-based food businesses, which are non-licensable, to ensure food safety standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I explained in my opening speech, SFA takes a risk-based approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Home-based food businesses are allowed by the Housing and Development Board and the Urban Redevelopment Authority to operate only on a small scale.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This limits the scale of food production and preparation, and food sold, making the associated food safety risks low.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As such, home-based food businesses are not required to be licensed by SFA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In response to Mr Keith Chua, SFA does not, therefore, track the number of home-based food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While there is no requirement to be licensed, home-based food businesses must not sell unsafe food or food prepared under unsanitary conditions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Directions can be given to a home-based food business to stop its activities if they are assessed to threaten food safety.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is the law today and the FSSB does not change this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These disallowed activities will be set out by SFA in regulations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These will consist of higher risk activities such as the supply of sashimi, which is uncooked.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The best way for home-based food businesses to ensure that food prepared and sold is safe for consumption is to observe food safety practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA has provided guidelines on food safety and hygiene practices for home-based food businesses online, and I encourage home-based food businesses to refer to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Home-based food businesses are also encouraged to enrol in food safety courses to be equipped with essential food safety knowledge and skills for correct food handling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A list of these courses, including those that are subsidised for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents by SkillsFuture Singapore, can be found on the MySkillsFuture website.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On food workers, Mr Don Wee said that both food businesses and workers should be held accountable to uphold food safety standards and expressed concern over decriminalising failures by food workers to attend training.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I agree wholeheartedly with Mr Don Wee that training in proper food handling is a key contributor to ensuring safe food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The approach taken under the FSSB considers that adequate training of food workers can be best ensured by the food business, which supervises and has oversight of its food workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It may not be reasonable to expect new food workers entering the industry to know what kind of training is required.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ensuring trained food workers is not a new responsibility for food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, licensed food businesses are already required to ensure their workers are trained before deploying them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The food worker directed will be committing an offence by refusing to go for the training.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Carrie Tan asked about our position on the sharing of produce from community gardens.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Whether this is considered as "supply" under the Bill would depend on the context.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In general, community gardens are small in scale and growers typically keep the produce for personal consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They may also sometimes share the fruits of their labour with their families and friends.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Bill makes an exception for such situations, as outlined in clause 8.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who produce edible plants at a larger scale, for sale or to distribute to others whom they do not have a personal relationship with, will be considered to be engaged in the activity of "supply".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The food safety and suitability requirements would hence apply to such groups.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Carrie Tan also asked if there are guidelines for those in the community who grow and share food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: NParks publishes online, good food safety practices when growing edibles.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who are interested can find out more on NParks' GardeningSG portal.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I explained before, we are taking a risk-based approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Regarding pesticides, there is a potential food safety risk from the transfer of harmful chemical residues and other contaminants to humans from the consumption of plants that are cultivated with the unsafe use of pesticides.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Pesticide misuse is a food safety concern and hence, the registration of pesticides used on edible plants and the certification of pesticide operators are covered under Part 11.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Lastly, the use of human excreta or raw animal or bird excreta as farm manure is prohibited to minimise food safety risks related to microbial contamination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Carrie Tan also asked if wild chickens can be integrated into community gardens to support local farming efforts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This matter is outside the scope of the Bill, but I will briefly address the question, with the Speaker's permission, of course, so as to keep this debate relevant to the House.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that explains why there are some prohibitions in place.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee expressed concern on the impact of food recalls on small businesses and asked if the Ministry could introduce assistance schemes to help them recover and stay operational.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And indeed, food recalls, while necessary to ensure that food products that are found to be unsafe for consumption do not remain in the market, can have costly consequences for food businesses, affecting their reputation, productivity and profit margin.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The potential impact from recalls would hopefully encourage greater vigilance by businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Traceability and record-keeping can help minimise the cost impact from recalls as they would be better able to identify the affected products and avoid having to recall more than necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The FSSB takes a calibrated approach by requiring only businesses that are key food distribution nodes to take on traceability and record-keeping, but businesses are encouraged to do so even if it is not required under the law.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Apart from strengthening food product traceability, food manufacturers, importers and distributors can scrutinise and verify partners and processes within their supply chain and ensure that food products comply with the relevant regulations, for example, food safety standards and proper labelling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These proactive actions can help to mitigate the likelihood of recalls.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Jean See asked about SFA's plans to ensure that food business licence applicants are made aware of and geared up to implement the Food Control Plan requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, food businesses are already required to meet prescriptive requirements to ensure food safety as part of their licensing requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Under the Bill, food businesses that are prescribed to require a Food Control Plan will have the flexibility to decide on the preventative measures suited to their operational needs, and this should not add significant compliance burden to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA will also provide information and guidance documents to facilitate compliance to regulations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Jean See asked if SFA takes into consideration past employment contraventions of food business licence applicants while assessing their suitability to operate food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As per clause 92, SFA will consider, among other factors, whether the applicant has been subject to regulatory action or convicted of relevant offences; whether the applicant or their associate is or was disqualified from holding the same licence or another licence; as well as the applicant's compliance history as it relates to the licensable food business.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the necessity of separating the health promotion provisions from the Sale of Food Act and including them in the Bill.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Minister of State Rahayu has addressed this in her opening speech earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I will not further talk about this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, on how the Bill will help us to prepare for emerging challenges in safeguarding food security.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There were a number of questions on the MSR.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan asked about the factors that MSE or SFA would consider in imposing MSR on entities dealing with essential food items other than rice, or agri-food production inputs; and in fixing the MSR quantity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Ms He Ting Ru also asked on the types of food which will be required to be maintained under the MSR, and if medium-term guidance can be given to MSR entities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Dennis Tan expressed concern with the potential impact of MSR on the food industry, including local farms and importers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the Ministry would put in place measures to ensure that MSR does not increase the risk of food wastage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In deciding whether to require certain industry players to hold a certain level of foods or agri-food production inputs in Singapore to mitigate the risk of agri-food supply disruptions, the DG (FS) will consider matters that can affect the supply resilience of essential food items or agri-food production inputs in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These matters are outlined in clause 18(1) and clause 25 and includes food security factors such as global food availability, local production capacity, and range of supply sources, which can affect the supply of the item, as well as local consumption patterns and preferences, which can influence the demand of the item.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Before the MSR is imposed, SFA will support relevant MSR entities in making preparations to ensure that they have the capacity to meet their MSR obligations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, the Government already works closely with the industry to maintain rice stocks under the Rice Stockpile Scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has served us well by ensuring that Singaporeans never face shortage, even during the COVID-19 pandemic when supply chains were disrupted.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For rice importers, the transitioning of the Rice Stockpile Scheme to the MSR scheme should pose minimal compliance burden to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Rather, the design of the MSR, such as the "daily MSR" and the "average MSR", aims to provide the industry with more operational flexibility.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will allow the rice importers to more effectively manage and churn their rice stocks, which will help to reduce wastage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Given that the rice stocks are commercially-owned, it will be in the commercial interest of the MSR entities to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ultimately, stockpiling provides a cushion against food supply disruptions and provides some degree of assurance to Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It also enhances our ability to manage the impacts of food supply disruptions by buying us time for supply chains to recover or to bring in alternative supplies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Such a scheme is akin to an insurance policy for food security and must naturally come with an insurance premium.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if the FMP will end up incurring higher costs for our local farms to adhere to the requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Instead, the farms are empowered to design and implement an FMP tailored to the specific needs of their business.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In my opening speech, I mentioned that farmers will need to come up with their methods and processes addressing the key areas of waste, feed, fish stocking, biosecurity and disease management.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Clearly, failing to plan is planning to fail.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our aquaculture farms have been hit by toxic algal blooms before and would know the devastation that this causes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With better management of farms, we expect that farms would be far less likely to experience such incidents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The FMP would also be important to promote sustainable farm practices and the long-term viability of farm sites.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Aquaculture players I spoke to agreed that a well-managed fish farm that protects the marine environment will also ensure the safety of other nearby farms and protect the industry as a whole.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: After all, they all share the same body of water.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farms are responsible for ensuring the processes in their FMP are followed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farms can revise the FMP, subject to SFA's agreement, to adapt to changing conditions or operational needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This flexibility helps farms to stay resilient and responsive to evolving challenges while maintaining necessary standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Earlier, I also mentioned that the FMP implementation will be phased to allow time for transition.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA will provide the necessary support to help existing farms adjust to the requirement to have an FMP, such as through SFA's collaboration with Temasek Polytechnic's Aquaculture Innovation Centre to conduct training to guide farms and the rolling out of the Aquatic Animal Health Service in August 2023.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Additionally, we have worked with the Singapore Standards Council on the development of Good Agricultural Practice, Good Aquaculture Practice, and Clean and Green standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These standards will provide valuable guidance that farms can refer to when developing and implementing their FMPs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While this is out of the scope of FSSB, I want to assure Members that SFA is committed to supporting our local farms to grow food in a productive, climate-resilient and resource-efficient way.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the years, we have increased support to our farms for energy-efficiency and productivity transformation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will also continue to support the industry in achieving greater offtake of local produce through various initiatives, such as working with the Singapore Agro-Food Enterprises Federation Limited to facilitate long-term commercial contracts between farmers and food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Third, on how we will support the industry and collaborate with stakeholders in the transition towards the updated food safety and security regime.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the concerns raised during consultation with the industry and how SFA and MSE incorporated the feedback into the Bill.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA has been engaging the industry since 2023 via a series of in-person engagement sessions, during the drafting of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Public consultation also took place in tranches between March and September 2024.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Public consultations on health promotion and marketing offences, led by MOH, received feedback from 17 respondents via REACH.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There was general support for the Bill's provisions and most comments related to clarifications on the scope of the requirements, for example, the responsibilities imposed on food delivery companies and when the new requirements would take effect.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA published responses to these questions on 11 November 2024.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have incorporated the feedback received in the Bill, where relevant.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This was in response to clarifications from the industry on the definition of "novel food".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We included a provision to allow Minister to declare by order in the Gazette any substance or a mixture of substances that are not plant pesticides.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This would allow the exclusion of predatory insects, predatory mites, parasitoids and nematodes that prey on and eliminate plant insects, from the definition of "plant pesticides".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the likely impact to the industry arising from the additional requirements and how the Government plans to facilitate the industry's transition towards the new regulatory framework.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee also asked if SFA will provide guidance, subsidies or transitional support to ease the burden of compliance costs on small food businesses to transition to the updated food safety regime.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I understand Members' concern about the potential cost impact of these requirements, especially for small businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, the implementation of the various measures in the Bill will be staged.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, the Bill provides flexibility for SFA to take a calibrated approach in imposing requirements to suit the operating context of different types of food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In prosecuting food safety lapses, SFA will also consider the impact on public health, such as the number of people affected, in prosecutions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The simplification and consistency that the Bill brings would reduce regulatory complexity for businesses, which would reduce the cost and compliance costs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I mentioned earlier, the food security requirements would also help businesses strengthen their resilience.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I had also shared some of the support measures SFA would implement to support the industry through the transition, such as guidance documents and training.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Businesses which need support in implementing systems, such as inventory management systems, could tap productivity-boosting technological solutions, such as the Industry Digital Plans launched by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Carrie Tan pointed out that collaborating with citizens would be beneficial for food resilience and asked if there are plans to evolve SFA's role beyond that of a regulator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, SFA today already plays a role beyond that of a regulator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA works closely with the industry to develop capabilities in various areas, from food safety measures to growing local produce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SFA also has public outreach programmes to educate the public about food safety and resilience matters, for example, the steps the public can take during food disruptions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Building food safety and security is a long-term endeavour, one that requires the collective effort of the Government, industry and consumers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Speaker, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon has addressed some of the Members' clarifications.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the supply of food that is past its labelled date is permissible under the Bill in any circumstances.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: An example cited was a retailer permitting an individual to take expired food for their individual consumption.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Food manufacturers locally and overseas use a variety of date marks on their packaging.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This includes date marks, such as "Use by" and "Best Before", which are used by different jurisdictions and are internationally accepted terms under the Codex General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To guide the future Subsidiary Legislation on date marking, SFA is conducting a study on the feasibility and implications of differentiating the various date marks, based on their relevance to food safety risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This would allow SFA to prescribe only date marks indicating that the food may have become unsafe for consumption as "outdated".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA targets to complete the study before the relevant Part of the Bill comes into force.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question about the Government's efforts on food waste reduction, this is not within the scope of the Bill, but I will briefly address the question, with Speaker's permission.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The preferred way to manage food waste is upstream, before the food becomes close to being "unsuitable" or "unsafe".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is in the interest of the businesses to optimise the turnover of their inventory and to minimise food waste and unsold food.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Retailers should contribute to reducing food waste in a safe manner, by ensuring surplus food given away is not "outdated".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how clause 144 of the Bill interacts with the Good Samaritan Food Donation Act and whether volunteers and donors will continue to be shielded from penalties for unintended oversights.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Yip also noted the penalties in clauses 29 to 31 and 144 to 146, and asked if exemptions and safeguards will be in place to protect well-intentioned individuals contributing to food security.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This Bill and the Good Samaritan Food Donation Act are complementary.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The purpose of the Good Samaritan Food Donation Act is to offer food donors protection from criminal liability, such as under clauses 144, 145 and 146, and civil liability, which would in turn encourage donation of surplus food and reduce food waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, the protection cannot be absolute as the health of the consumers, similarly, needs protection.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, section 4 of the Good Samaritan Food Donation Act outlined the conditions that donors have to comply with.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To better support food donors, SFA will be publishing an updated Guidelines for Food Donation on its website later this month.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The guidelines will contain a list of food safety practices to help food donors ensure that their donated food is safe for consumption.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, maintaining a process to check that the food they are donating is safe and suitable for consumption; and adhering to safe food handling requirements, such as temperature control and hygienic food handling practices.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA will continue to engage food donor bodies to raise awareness on safe food donation-related matters, including proper understanding of date labels on food products.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the measures to prevent the entry of contaminated or non-compliant food products under the private consumption limit.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA takes a risk-based approach to our food safety regime.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The allowable limit under the private consumption takes into consideration the small quantity which limits its distribution potential and food safety risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, we recognise that some food types, such as game meat or animal blood products, could pose greater risk to consumers and public health.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Such food are of higher regulatory concern and are not allowed to be brought in under the private consumption limit.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We encourage consumers to exercise caution when purchasing food from overseas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA will raise public awareness on the potential food safety risks associated with consuming overseas food products brought in by travellers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if the Bill permits the selling, gifting or donation of excess food brought in under the private consumption allowance and whether SFA has the capability to enforce the prohibition of selling the food brought in under private consumption.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: He also suggested collaborations with e-commerce platforms to monitor and regulate transactions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Gifting of such food is also restricted to that carried out as part of a personal relationship, as distribution beyond which, such as through sale or donation channels, will increase the food safety risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Consumers should exercise discretion and only purchase what they can reasonably consume.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA will monitor the situation and review our enforcement periodically.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Don Wee expressed concerns about the mass food poisoning cases last year and asked about the preventive measures the Bill will introduce to assure consumers on food safety.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked whether there are other efforts to promote food safety besides penalties and licence suspensions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA adopts a science-based risk management approach to safeguard food safety, consistent with international standards.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of SFA’s import control regime, SFA accredits import sources for higher-risk food such as meat and eggs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA then inspects, samples, and tests food imports based on their risk profile, and may require the treatment, destruction or re-export of food that fails checks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the retail level, food businesses such as restaurants and caterers must ensure cleanliness of their premises and the safe preparation and handling of food.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA may impose certain requirements on licensed food businesses, such as on the design and cleanliness of the premises or equipment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Similarly, taking a risk-based approach, SFA will conduct inspections based on risk profiles of the premises and food sold, and track records of past infringements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Bill will also require food businesses to put in place upstream preventive measures through Food Control Plans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA works closely with sectoral agencies, such as the Early Childhood Development Agency for preschools and MOH for nursing homes, on guidelines and regulations to protect these communities from food safety incidents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This includes the sharing of good food handling practices and food safety management systems such as the design and management of in-house kitchens to uphold food safety practices.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA also conducts training for sectoral agencies, to strengthen their capabilities in assessing food safety risks associated with food production and preparation on their premises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA requires food businesses to ensure that their employees have adequate capability in ensuring food safety.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: All employees who handle food must be trained and have passed the Workforce Skills Qualifications Food Safety Course Level 1 before carrying on work as a food worker.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Food businesses with higher food safety risk, such as caterers, are also required to appoint Food Hygiene Officers to assist the food businesses in establishing and maintaining proper food safety system.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Don Wee asked how we are calibrating the penalties to ensure that they are neither excessively punitive for small businesses nor too lenient to deter large offenders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The penalties are intended to deter egregious behaviour to safeguard public health.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hence, the penalty framework is organised around severity and threat to public health, culpability of offences and circumstances of the breach, instead of size of business.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While the Bill puts in place the penalty framework, ultimately the actual penalty for each offence will be decided by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To avoid being overly punitive, lapses of less serious nature, such as a breach of licensing conditions, will be decriminalised.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, such transgressions will still be subjected to penalties under SFA’s licensing framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: On the expanded scope of directions, Ms Jean See asked about the type of checks that the authorised officer or food inspector might undertake to determine if a food vending machine is in unclean or unsanitary condition as to make any food from the machine unsafe or unsuitable, or likely to be unsafe or unsuitable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: She also suggested for SFA to consider requiring vending machine operators to display on the machine the most recent date the machine was cleaned, and for highly perishable food, the “sell-by” date.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA takes a risk-based approach to regulating food vending machines.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Operators of food vending machines are required to hold SFA licences if the machines have in-machine food processing functions, or sell raw meat or seafood, given the higher potential food safety risks involved.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under the Bill, licensed operators will be required to put in place a Food Control Plan, which would include regular cleaning and maintenance regime to ensure the machine is kept in clean, hygienic, and good working condition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Companies may wish to adopt Ms See’s suggestion of displaying the most recent date of cleaning, to better track the implementation of their cleaning regime.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Operators must also display their SFA licence and contact number on the machines to facilitate the provision of feedback by the public.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA conducts checks on food vending machines, to ensure food safety.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This includes ensuring that the machines are clean, pest-free and that the storage temperatures within the machines are in accordance with the regulations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA will investigate if there are suspected food safety lapses and, where necessary, take the relevant enforcement actions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While we have come far in this journey, the food industry has and will continue to see new opportunities, and face new challenges.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I call on all Members of the House to give your support to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Does any Member have clarifications for the two Ministries?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister I think this is one of the thickest Bills we have had for a while.
